In the main experiments, the persona number $N$ is set to 4. The advanced LLM we use to construct training data for both persona generation and rationale generation is GPT-4o-mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18).6 MPAQ is fine-tuned on Llama-3.1-8B via LoRA.7 We fix the batch size to 16, lora_r to 32, lora_alpha to 64, with all dropout rates set to 0.1. Greedy decoding is used for generation, with default hyper-parameters in the Transformers library.8 The two stages of MPAQ are trained separately. In stage 1, we train the model for 2 epochs with a learning rate of 1e-4 on IBM-ArgQ-5.3kArgs and 3 epochs with a learning rate of 1e-4 on IBM-Rank-30k. In stage 2, we train the model for 2

epochs with a learning rate of 8e-5 on IBM-ArgQ-5.3kArgs and 2 epochs with a learning rate of 2e-5 on IBM-Rank-30k. These hyper-parameters are obtained through hyper-parameter search (See § A.15 for details). The regressor head is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer. All results in the main experiments are averaged across three independent runs with different random seeds.

candidate_windows.section_title: impact of different advanced llms for training data construction
candidate_windows.normalized_section_title: impact of different advanced llms for training data construction
candidate_windows.window_text:
Since we use an advanced LLM to construct the training data for both persona and rationale generation, this advanced LLM can be viewed as a teacher model for training MPAQ. Here, we explore the performance of MPAQ on IBM-Rank-30k dataset using different teacher models for training data construction. Besides GPT-4o-mini used in our main experiments, we also experiment with GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as teacher models. The results are listed in Table 4. Among the teacher models evaluated, GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct demonstrate comparable performance across all evaluation metrics, while GPT-3.5-Turbo shows relatively weaker performance. Notably, MPAQ consistently outperforms the baseline methods regardless of the teacher model used, demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

![](images/2feae5b4c507c7d2e97cc05610783a56bad0eb0035ad24dc3f5e4beb2da065fe.jpg)

Figure 7: Personas distribution and diversity analysis: (a) The top 15 most commonly generated personas; (b) Distribution of the number of unique personas generated per topic (mean = 19.70).

In our main experiments, we follow the official data split of IBM-Rank-30k, which represents a cross-topic setting where the topics in validation and test sets have no overlap with those in the training set. To further evaluate MPAQ's capabilities, we also conduct experiments in an in-topic setting by randomly splitting the entire dataset, allowing arguments from the same topics to appear in both training and testing.

As shown in Table 10, while all methods demonstrate relatively stronger performance in the intopic setting, MPAQ consistently outperforms the

basielines across most metrics in both settings.

candidate_windows.section_title: experimental settings for human and gpt evaluations
candidate_windows.normalized_section_title: experimental settings for human and gpt evaluations
candidate_windows.window_text:
To evaluate the generation quality of MPAQ compared to its teacher model GPT-4o-mini, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation using both human annotators and GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20). Our evaluation focuses on both persona generation and rationale generation capabilities.

Evaluation Data Preparation We randomly sample 50 test examples from IBM-Rank-30k dataset. For each example, we obtain two sets of generations: one from MPAQ and one from GPT4o-mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18) using identical prompts from Tables 15 and 17. These generations are paired to create 50 comparison pairs, with the order of MPAQ and GPT-4o-mini outputs randomized within each pair.

Evaluation Process We employ two independent evaluation approaches:

- Human Evaluation: Two annotators, graduate students in the field of artificial intelligence, independently assess each comparison pair to determine which system produces better personas and rationales. Any disagreements between annotators are resolved through discussion sessions. The interface is shown in Figure 9.   
- GPT-4o Evaluation: We use GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20) with a carefully designed evaluation prompt (Table 19) to judge which system

generates better personas and rationales for each comparison pair.

We conduct in-context learning (ICL) experiments using three different LLMs: GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. For each model, we evaluate its performance with varying numbers of demonstrations (0-shot, 1-shot, 2-shot, and 4-shot) on both datasets. The results are shown in Table 14.

We observe that increasing the number of demonstrations does not lead to clear improvements in the models' ICL performance on argument quality assessment. We hypothesize this is due to the subjective nature of the task, making it difficult for models to learn effective evaluation abilities from a limited number of demonstrations. Notably, these ICL results substantially underperform our fine-tuned approach, highlighting the importance of task-specific training for argument quality assessment.

candidate_windows.normalized_section_title: more implementation details for the main experiments
candidate_windows.window_text:
During training, we conduct a random hyperparameter search. For 2 stages on both IBM-Rank-30k and IBM-ArgQ-5.3kArgs datasets, we set the learning rate search range to $[2e - 5,4e - 5,8e - 5,1e - 4,2e - 4]$ and the epoch search range to

[1, 2, 3]. Ultimately, for Stage 1, we select the hyper-parameters that minimize the auto-regressive loss on the validation set. For Stage 2, we choose the hyper-parameters that maximize the Pearson correlation coefficient on the validation set.

In this work, GPT series models are accessed through the official API provided by OpenAI. Other open-source models are obtained from Huggingface.

Pearson, Spearman correlation coefficients and Kendall's Tau evaluation metrics are calculated using the python SciPy library, while the other metrics are evaluated using the python scikit-learn library.

review_flags.evidence:
Since we use an advanced LLM to construct the training data for both persona and rationale generation, this advanced LLM can be viewed as a teacher model for training MPAQ. Here, we explore the performance of MPAQ on IBM-Rank-30k dataset using different teacher models for training data construction. Besides GPT-4o-mini used in our main experiments, we also experiment with GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as teacher models. The results are listed in Table 4. Among the teacher models evaluated, GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct demonstrate comparable performance across all evaluation metrics, while GPT-3.5-Turbo shows relatively weaker performance. review_flags.section_title: experimental settings for human and gpt evaluations
review_flags.evidence:
To evaluate the generation quality of MPAQ compared to its teacher model GPT-4o-mini, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation using both human annotators and GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20). Our evaluation focuses on both persona generation and rationale generation capabilities.

Evaluation Data Preparation We randomly sample 50 test examples from IBM-Rank-30k dataset. For each example, we obtain two sets of generations: one from MPAQ and one from GPT4o-mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18) using identical prompts from Tables 15 and 17. These generations are paired to create 50 comparison pairs, with the order of MPAQ and GPT-4o-mini outputs randomized within each pair.

Evaluation Process We employ two independent evaluation approaches:

- Human Evaluation: Two annotators, graduate students in the field of artificial intelligence, independently assess each comparison pair to determine which system produces better personas and rationales. Any disagreements between annotators are resolved through discussion sessions. The interface is shown in Figure 9.   
- GPT-4o Evaluation: We use GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20) with a carefully designed evaluation prompt (Table 19) to judge which system

generates better personas and rationales for each comparison pair.

We conduct in-context learning (ICL) experiments using three different LLMs: GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. For each model, we evaluate its performance with varying numbers of demonstrations (0-shot, 1-shot, 2-shot, and 4-shot) on both datasets. The results are shown in Table 14.

We observe that increasing the number of demonstrations does not lead to clear improvements in the models' ICL performance on argument quality assessment. We hypothesize this is due to the subjective nature of the task, making it difficult for models to learn effective evaluation abilities from a limited number of demonstrations. Notably, these ICL results substantially underperform our fine-tuned approach, highlighting the importance of task-specific training for argument quality assessment.

Bojun Jin $^{1}$ , Jianzhu Bao $^{1*}$ , Yufang Hou $^{2}$ , Yang Sun $^{1,3}$ , Yice Zhang $^{1}$ , Huajie Wang $^{1}$ , Bin Liang $^{4}$ , Ruifeng Xu $^{1,3,5*}$

# Abstract

Argument quality assessment faces inherent challenges due to its subjective nature, where different evaluators may assign varying quality scores for an argument based on personal perspectives. Although existing datasets collect opinions from multiple annotators to model subjectivity, most existing computational methods fail to consider multi-perspective evaluation. To address this issue, we propose MPAQ, a multi-persona framework for argument quality assessment that simulates diverse evaluator perspectives through large language models. It first dynamically generates targeted personas tailored to an input argument, then simulates each persona's reasoning process to evaluate the argument quality from multiple perspectives. To effectively generate fine-grained quality scores, we develop a coarse-to-fine scoring strategy that first generates a coarse-grained integer score and then refines it into a fine-grained decimal score. Experiments on IBM-Rank-30k and IBM-ArgQ-5.3kArgs datasets demonstrate that MPAQ consistently outperforms strong baselines while providing comprehensive multi-perspective rationales.

# 1 Introduction

Argument quality assessment, a fundamental task in computational argumentation, aims to automatically evaluate the persuasiveness and validity of arguments in natural language texts (Wachsmuth et al., 2017; Gienapp et al., 2020; Wachsmuth et al., 2024). It plays a crucial role in multiple domains, such as automatic essay scoring (Persing and Ng, 2013; Nguyen and Litman, 2018; Ding et al., 2023), writing support (Stab and Gurevych, 2014, 2017), and argument generation (Slonim et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024). This subjective nature of argument quality assessment has been well-recognized and carefully considered in data collection efforts. This limitation motivates us to rethink the design of argument quality assessment methods: instead of pursuing a single universal standard, we should embrace multiple perspectives in quality prediction, similar to how human annotators approach this task. Inspired by recent advances in leveraging large language models (LLMs) for persona simulation (Tseng et al., 2024), we propose utilizing LLMs' role-playing capabilities to assess argument quality from multiple personas' perspectives, thereby obtaining more comprehensive and accurate quality predictions. Finally, the predicted scores from all personas are aggregated into an overall quality score. # 2 Related Work

# 2.1 Argument Quality Assessment

The definition of argument quality is a complex problem, and many studies have conducted exploration on this question (Swanson et al., 2015; Wachsmuth et al., 2016; Joshi et al., 2023; Fromm et al., 2023). Building on a comprehensive summary of previous work (Hamblin, 1970; Johnson and Blair, 1977; Aristotle and Kennedy, 1991; Eemeren and Grootendorst, 2003), Wachsmuth et al. (2017) proposed a taxonomy of argumentation quality with three major dimensions: logic, rhetoric, and dialectic. According to their definitions, logic focuses on whether the argument is built on acceptable and relevant premises that are sufficient to support the conclusion, while rhetoric assesses the argument's ability to persuade the intended audience of the author's stance, and dialectic examines whether the argument contributes meaningfully and acceptably to resolving the issue for the target audience. Based on this method, they also constructed an argument quality dataset containing approximately 5.3k arguments annotated with the overall quality scores. Gretz et al. # 3.1 Stage 1: Persona Generation

This stage aims to generate diverse and relevant persona information based on the input argument $a$ and topic $t$ . To develop this capability in MPAQ, we leverage advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2023)) to construct training data, following existing studies in data synthesis (Wang et al., 2024; Long et al., 2024). We use carefully crafted prompt (Table 15 in Appendix C) to instruct an advanced LLM to generate diverse and relevant persona information for each input argument. Some examples are shown in Figure 2 (Stage 1). By incorporating analytical

Our goal here is to train an LLM that takes an argument $a$ , a topic $t$ and a specific persona $P_i$ as input, then simultaneously predicts a fine-grained persona-specific decimal quality score $s_i^{f,p}$ and generates corresponding textual rationales $r_i^s$ and $r_i^w$ . However, our preliminary analysis (shown as

"Llama-Text-Score" in Table 2) reveals that simply training an LLM to generate such fine-grained decimal scores (e.g., 0.7554) with rationales in text format yields poor accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a coarse-to-fine scoring strategy that consists of two steps: (1) the LLM first generates a coarse-grained integer score (0-9) $s_i^{c,p}$ and corresponding rationales in text format; (2) the coarse-grained score $s_i^{c,p}$ is then refined into a fine-grained decimal score $s_i^{f,p}$ through a regression head $f_{\mathrm{reg}}$ . Specifically, the prompt template we use for this process is shown in Table 1. This coarse-to-fine scoring strategy can be formalized as:

$$
s _ {i} ^ {c, p}, r _ {i} ^ {s}, r _ {i} ^ {w} = \operatorname {L L M} _ {\theta^ {a}} (a, t, P _ {i}) \tag {2}
$$

$$
s _ {i} ^ {f, p} = f _ {\operatorname {r e g}} \left(\operatorname {E m b} \left(s _ {i} ^ {c, p}\right)\right) \tag {3}
$$

where $\mathrm{LLM}_{\theta^a}(\cdot)$ is the fine-tuned LLM for persona-specific quality assessment, $\mathrm{Emb}(s_i^{c,p})$ denotes the LLM-encoded token embedding of $s_i^{c,p}$ .

During training, the coarse-grained score label is derived from the fine-grained score using:

$$
s _ {i} ^ {c} = \min  (\left\lfloor s _ {i} ^ {f} \times 1 0 \right\rfloor , 9) \tag {4}
$$

where $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$ denotes the floor function. This ensures the coarse-grained score stays within the range [0, 9]. The training objective is the sum of two losses: (1) a standard language modeling loss for coarse-grained score and rationale generation; (2) a mean absolute error (MAE) loss for fine-grained score prediction. Note that during training, all personaspecific scores $s_i^{f,p}$ share the same training label $s^f$ due to our indirect supervision strategy. Despite using the same labels across different personas, we believe the trained model can make differentiated coarse- and fine-grained quality predictions by incorporating persona information and rationales as context during inference. We empirically validate this hypothesis through experiments in $\S$ A.10.

In this manner, we fine-tune the same small LLM as in § 3.1 to obtain another LoRA adapter $\theta^a$ with a regression head that is responsible for producing fine-grained quality scores.

# 4.6 Ablation Study

To validate the effectiveness of different components in MPAQ, we conduct ablation studies on

both datasets, as shown in Table 3.

Impact of Persona Design. First, removing the multi-persona framework while retaining the coarse-to-fine scoring strategy ("w/o Multi-persona") leads to substantial performance drops on both datasets, highlighting the importance of incorporating multiple perspectives. "w/o Dynamic Persona Generation", which removes Stage 1 entirely and uses fixed personas instead, shows performance degradation, validating the effectiveness of our persona generation stage. Additionally, removing analytical perspectives in Stage 1 ("w/o Analytical Perspectives") or replacing the structured strengths and weaknesses analysis with unrestricted analysis in Stage 2 ("w/o Strengths & Weaknesses") both lead to decreased performance, indicating that these detailed specifications help guide more accurate quality assessment.

Impact of Scoring Strategy. "w/o Coarse-to-fine Scoring", which replaces the coarse-grained score with a static token before fine-grained prediction, shows performance decreases across both datasets. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our hierarchical scoring strategy.

Impact of Architecture Design. Both architectural variants show decreased performance: "w/o Two-stage Design", which concatenates persona generation and quality assessment into a single inference pipeline, and "w/o Two LoRA Adapters", which employs a shared adapter for both stages. These results validate our design decision to maintain separate stages with dedicated LoRA adapters, allowing for more focused parameter optimization for each specific task.

# 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a multi-persona framework for argument quality assessment (MPAQ). It simulates diverse evaluator perspectives through LLMs to model the inherent subjectivity in argument quality assessment. Extensive experiments on two big datasets (IBM-Rank-30k and IBM-ArgQ-5.3kArgs) demonstrate MPAQ's superior performance compared to several strong baselines.

# Limitations

While our method demonstrates superior performance, it incurs additional computational overhead due to the increased data volume from our two-stage process and multi-perspective evaluation framework. Nevertheless, we consider this computational trade-off worthwhile given the significant performance improvements achieved.

Furthermore, since our method requires a reasonable amount of training data, we evaluate our model on the two largest argument quality assessment datasets. Adapting our framework to medium-sized argument quality datasets on different quality dimensions is left for future work.

Finally, due to the absence of annotator profile information in argument quality assessment datasets, we could not directly evaluate the generated personas and their corresponding argument quality scores. Future work should compare the generated persona information with real-world data.

Any disagreements between annotators are resolved through discussion sessions. The interface is shown in Figure 9. - GPT-4o Evaluation: We use GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20) with a carefully designed evaluation prompt (Table 19) to judge which system generates better personas and rationales for each comparison pair. # A.13 Generation Quality of Teacher Model Since we use the personas and rationales generated by GPT-4o-mini, the generation quality of GPT-4o-mini is significant for training MPAQ. Therefore, we conduct a human evaluation of the personas and rationales generated by GPT-4o-mini.
